southern-democratic-nominee-withdraws.summary: With Breckinridge out of the race, candidates outside the two parties take 25.2% of the vote, against 38.8% in 1860, and the two-party split moves 10.0 points toward Douglas. Alabama, Arkansas, California, Delaware and 11 more flip, but Lincoln still wins, 173–122–8. The closest call is Illinois, which holds for Lincoln by 3.3 points. Douglas wins in 0 of 100 draws. Extremely low confidence. The interviews point the other way from the historical record.
assumptions: The Southern Democratic ticket is removed from the ballot and its voters redistribute among the remaining candidates, with most going to the Northern Democratic nominee and some to the Constitutional Union candidate or staying home.
howIGotThis: What changed: The nominee of the Southern wing of the divided administration party leaves the race, leaving the Northern wing's nominee as the party's only standard-bearer.

What historians found (11 findings, strong evidence): No source models Breckinridge withdrawing. Evidence suggests Southern voters would not have moved to Douglas: the 1860 contest was split by section, Douglas polled weakly in the South, and fusion tickets in the North and Texas did poorly or split. Analogues from 1856, 1912 and 1924 are loose.
The numbers: the 1860 census counts and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1860 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.
Extremely low confidence: The interviews point the other way from the historical record.

findings.claim: Beating Lincoln required fusing the three opposing parties, carrying a solid South and three or four Northern states. Barriers to fusion were formidable, and Southern fire-eaters wanted the split.

sources.title: Election of 1860

findings.claim: The 1860 campaign was two contests: Lincoln vs Douglas in the North, Breckinridge vs Bell in the South. Douglas had no hope in ten Southern states, so a Breckinridge exit would not obviously help Douglas.

sources.title: Election of 1860

findings.claim: The only Southern fusion, a joint Bell–Douglas ticket in Texas, won just 24 percent against Breckinridge, so anti-Breckinridge voters did not consolidate effectively behind Douglas.

sources.title: Election of 1860

findings.claim: Vote totals: Lincoln 1,866,452; Douglas 1,382,713; Breckinridge 847,953; Bell 592,906. Turnout was about 82 percent of eligible northern men and 70 percent of southern men. A combined opposition would not by itself have beaten Lincoln.

before.quote: The Republican means to keep the territories free and protect working men's wages with fair tariffs. That's what matters to folk like us here.
before.reason: Harry Tate is a wage-earner in Illinois who qualifies under the state's property or tax-paying requirement to vote. His economic interests align with the protective tariff platform of Lincoln, which promises good wages for workers. The sectional crisis over slavery's expansion into territories is the dominant issue of the election, and K's unambiguous opposition to slavery's spread in free territories reflects the Republican ascendancy in Illinois.

after.quote: The Republican's talk of good wages and keeping slavery out of new lands sits right with me. I aim to vote tomorrow.
after.reason: Harry Tate qualifies to vote under Illinois property or tax requirements. As a mill or workshop wage-earner in a Northern industrial town, he would be drawn to the Republican nominee's platform of barring slavery from territories and raising protective tariffs to secure good wages for workers. The recent Southern Democratic withdrawal and consolidation behind the Northern Democrat candidate may discourage turnout slightly among those who saw the party as split, but Tate's economic interests and the Republican emphasis on worker prosperity make voting likely.

before.quote: The Republican's talk of good wages speaks to me. A man working for daily bread needs industry and fair dealing, not the slave question tearing the country apart.
before.reason: James Hayes qualifies to vote under Arkansas law and will almost certainly go to the polls. As a wage earner in a mill or workshop, the tariff platform of Lincoln—securing good wages for workers and fair prices for farmers—directly appeals to his material interests. The slave question, while divisive, touches him less immediately than the promise of economic protection.

after.quote: The Republican's talk of protecting wages and keeping the territories free sounds right to me, though I worry what comes after tomorrow.
after.reason: James Hayes is a wage laborer in Arkansas who qualifies to vote under state property or tax requirements. His economic interests and concerns about slavery's expansion into territories where free labor might compete align most closely with the Republican nominee's platform on tariffs and territorial freedom, though the crisis atmosphere and local social pressure in Arkansas create some uncertainty.

before.quote: I mean to vote for the Republican tomorrow. He will keep the territories free and let honest labor prosper without slaves undercutting the working man.
before.reason: Harry Ellis is a property-owning white man in Illinois who qualifies to vote and lives in a free state where the Republican Party's anti-slavery position for territories aligns with the economic and political views of his community. At 68, he is likely settled in his views, though the gravity of the moment and talk of disunion may give him some pause about whether K's compromise approach might preserve the Union.

after.quote: I mean to vote for the Republican tomorrow. He'll keep the territories free and see that working men get fair wages. That's what Illinois needs.
after.reason: Harry Ellis, a property-owning tradesman in Illinois, qualifies to vote and has strong incentives to cast a ballot. The Republican nominee Lincoln aligns with Northern industrial interests that benefit his class and region, promises protective tariffs for worker wages and farm prices, and opposes slavery in the territories—positions consistent with Illinois free-state sentiment. The recent consolidation of the Northern Democratic wing behind Douglas, while reducing that ticket's strength, has not shifted Ellis's preference.

before.quote: The Republican will keep the factories running and protect our wages from cheap slave labor competing in the territories. That's what matters to a working man like me.
before.reason: Ernest Reed is a mill and workshop worker in Massachusetts who depends on steady wages and fair prices. Lincoln's platform of high tariffs to encourage Northern industry and secure good wages for workers directly appeals to his material interests and class position, while his opposition to slavery's expansion into territories aligns with the free-labor ideology dominant in Massachusetts.

after.quote: The Republican's got the right idea on the territories and keeping wages up here. That's what matters for a man like me.
after.reason: Ernest Reed is a working man in a Massachusetts mill town where protective tariffs and free-soil policies align with his material interests in stable wages and Northern industrial development. The Republican nominee's clear opposition to slavery's expansion into territories and his economic platform for workers' prosperity match Reed's circumstances and values, though some uncertainty remains about whether the administration party's Northern nominee might better protect working men's interests.

The consolidation of the Northern administration faction behind Douglas, combined with the Republican nominee's (Lincoln's) platform on free territories, tariff protection for industry and farm prices, and firm union stance, aligns with the interests and values of a Northern agricultural household in this critical moment.
